cards.title: Choose one overarching goal and translate it into a measurable target
cards.summary: Run a forced-choice goal-setting debate that narrows many candidate goals to a single overarching one, then convert it into a specific number with a deadline.
cards.use_when: Setting the store's quarterly or annual priority — deciding whether to optimize for revenue, market share, new customers, repeat customers, or margin.
steps: List all candidate goals people actually care about (revenue, market share, new customers, cost containment, retention). Ask the team to argue each one out loud rather than jumping to consensus.

Force the group to a single answer by testing each candidate: cost containment fails because 'if we don't find a way to make money, avoiding spending it does us no good'; revenue fails if cash is not the actual constraint. The goal with the most downstream value (new customers, references, follow-on sales, employee confidence, press attention) is the one to test hardest.
Push past euphemisms — if someone renames 'market share' as 'more good customers,' make them state whether the measure is genuinely different or the same thing.

Once one goal remains, convert it into a number with a deadline. Set the number yourself after hearing everyone's input, and state plainly that the team will not fully agree and that there is no science here.

Explain the tradeoff you rejected and why to the people whose input you overruled — e.g. too few deals fails because 'our competitors are doing more than double that, and the analysts will throw up all over us.'
Write the goal in a bounded form including a quality qualifier, e.g. 'N new customers by a fixed date, at least M of whom will act as active references.'
Only after the number is fixed, spend the follow-on block mapping what each function (marketing, finance, engineering, sales) must do to make that number possible.
caveats: The source's specific figure (18 new customers, 10 references) is a fictional case illustration, not a benchmark.
A CEO unilaterally setting the number works when there is no data to decide; in a smaller store, the equivalent is that someone owns the call rather than averaging everyone's wishes.
Picking one goal does not cancel other goals — revenue goals still exist, they are simply not the ultimate measure this period.

cards.title: Depth beats breadth for new stores: pick one critical goal
cards.summary: A team can hold one overarching goal at a time; multiple simultaneous priorities dilute focus and stall execution.
cards.use_when: Deciding what the next 90 days of store work is actually for — product range expansion, ad spend, SEO, retention — before allocating budget or headcount.
steps: Ask what would still matter if the store hit every other metric. New customer acquisition that produces references, follow-on purchases, employee confidence and press interest is usually a stronger candidate than raw revenue or cost control in an early-stage business.
Introduce the anchor line to the team: 'If everything is important, then nothing is.' Use it to stop parallel initiatives competing for the same person's week.
Name the single priority in one sentence and get each function to justify what it contributes to it, rather than defending its own separate metric.
Reject substitutes that sound different but are the same measure (e.g. 'more good customers' vs 'market share').
When the priority is set, hold the line that other metrics are secondary until the period ends, and say so explicitly to the people who will be measured on them.
caveats: This is presented as a leadership stance in the source, not a universal law; businesses in maintenance mode or with a profitable core may legitimately run multiple balanced goals.
Choosing one goal privileges the stage of the business — an unproven store plausibly needs customers before it optimizes retention or margin.

cards.title: Beliefs and confidences surface constantly — plan for the relapse
cards.summary: After an intense planning or strategy session, expect visible enthusiasm on the day and a rapid return to old behavior within days; plan a follow-up session before the first one ends.
cards.use_when: Scheduling a strategy offsite, brand workshop or planning day for an ecommerce team and deciding whether one session is enough.
steps: Accept that the first session produces agreement, not change; recognize the 'typical first response' of distance and quiet in the days after.

Stop asking whether the session was worth it on the day. Measure the effect later by whether the agreed behaviors appear in ordinary work: joint meetings, unprompted cross-functional cooperation, people asking each other for input.
Book the next working session before the current one closes. If the team proposes skipping it because 'we should just see how things go,' treat that as a signal to hold the session, not cancel it.

Use the gap between sessions to state explicitly what you will and won't tolerate — e.g. intolerance of ego-driven behavior, willingness to challenge, requirement to hold each other accountable — so the standard is public before the relapse.
Expect one or more visible casualties: in the source, a senior team member quits between sessions. Protracted difficulty is normal for this stage.
Prepare for the possibility that the relapse is severe enough that a person who appeared committed leaves; hold the process anyway.
caveats: The source presents this as a recurring pattern in leadership, not a measured average; the sequence is illustrative.
The 'one colleague wouldn't be around by the next session' prediction is a plot device, not a forecast method.

cards.title: Diagnose whether each leader's 'first team' is their department or the company
cards.summary: Ask each departmental leader directly who they confide in and prioritize, because loyalties to a department over the company produce gatekeeping and information leaks.
cards.use_when: Investigating why store functions (merchandising, marketing, fulfillment, paid media) undermine each other, withhold information, or refuse to back company priorities over their own team's comfort.
steps: Ask the direct question: what did you tell your people about the strategy, and do you consider your own team more important than the leadership group you sit on?

Watch for the answer 'my staff is my first team, I'd do anything for them.' That is not the problem by itself — the problem is the consequence: managers become go-betweens, keep bad news local, and trade company commitments for departmental goodwill.

Explain the specific cost: when good managers don't act like a team, the company gets confusion about who the first team is. In retail terms, the buyer optimizes assortment, the marketer optimizes reach, and nobody owns the customer outcome.

Do not ask anyone to abandon or dismantle their own functional team; be explicit that the ask is that the company team becomes primary while department loyalties become secondary. For many people that will feel like abandonment, and saying so honestly keeps the demand credible.

Expose leaks by naming the observable fact — e.g. a staff member outside the leadership group knows the detail of an internal decision — then ask what the default should be for what is shared and what stays internal.
Hold that judgment comes before loyalty: putting team results ahead of individual or departmental issues is the last and often the hardest test.
caveats: Departments are not automatically wrong; the source keeps the point that departmental loyalty is valuable, it just cannot override company commitments.
For a small store where one person is both buyer and marketer, the 'first team' conflict takes a different form — usually founder versus contractor priorities rather than departmental turf.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Make the team's shared goal the actual agenda of every staff meeting
cards.summary: A recurring meeting should be dominated by working the shared critical number, not by status updates or touchy-feely exercises.
cards.use_when: Engineering a weekly or fortnightly ecommerce ops meeting that currently produces no decisions and no progress on the store's most important number.
steps: Open with a short review of each person's work, then spend most of the meeting on the single agreed goal — the source example is laying groundwork for the agreed number of new deals.

Decompose the goal into a short list of key drivers and track each in the meeting. In the source: product demonstrations, competitor analysis, sales training, product brochures. In a store this could be: landing page tests, competitor price/assortment analysis, ads team training, PDP photography.
Assign every driver to one named owner with a date. The owner reports progress, blockers and whether they are ahead or behind, without spinning.

When an owner says they haven't started because other people were not responsive, do not resolve it for them. Ask which named people are the blocker, and treat the owner's failure to escalate earlier as the live issue.
Note that some people are hard to hold accountable because they are helpful, defensive or intimidating. Name the pattern and use the easiest case as the example so the standard is visible.
Close each item with a decision or a reassignment, and start the next meeting from the same driver list.
caveats: The source's agenda sequence is a story illustration; adapt the number and driver list to the store's actual bottleneck.
Avoid exercising the process with no substance — the source deliberately replaces 'exercises' with real issues because abstractions produce polite agreement.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Define trust as willingness to be pushed, not as assuming alignment
cards.summary: Accountability between colleagues is not distrust; trust is knowing the push comes from caring about the outcome.
cards.use_when: Fixing a store team that avoids challenging each other about slip, quality, or stalled work — e.g. late product photography, unvalidated ad spend, unshipped collections.
steps: Separate two things that get conflated: trust is not 'we all assume everyone is on the same page and needs no pushing.' Trust is knowing that when a colleague pushes you, it is because they care about the team.
Instruct people to push with respect and under the working assumption that the other person is probably doing the right thing — but to push anyway and never hold back.
Model the smallest useful push: 'which of my people aren't available?' rather than an accusation; make the blocked owner name names and the blocking function describe its priorities out loud.
After the push, have the blocking party state what they will do about staffing and priority so the fix is owned rather than implied.
Apply the same standard to yourself where the useful store implication exists — it is not easy to hold anyone accountable, including people who are always helpful.
Expect visible discomfort and do not treat it as failure of the process.
caveats: The line that every team member should push 'never hold back' is the source's prescription inside a committed leadership group; it is a cultural standard, not a license for public criticism of individuals who are absent.
Hard-to-hold-accountable people are categorized in the source as helpful, defensive or intimidating — treat that as an observation, not a diagnostic instrument.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Handle destructive behavior inside the meeting and ask the offender to choose the venue
cards.summary: A leader who allows public attacks and disengagement to pass effectively endorses them; ask the offender whether to resolve the issue publicly or privately, then follow through.
cards.use_when: A store meeting breaks down — someone insults an absent colleague, mocks another function, or walks out mid-agenda — and the decision is whether to correct it now or later.
steps: Name the behavior without venting: 'don't ever slam a teammate who isn't in the room' and require the offender to make it right with that person directly.
Offer the choice of venue — public or one-on-one — so the offender owns the setting rather than being cornered. In the source, the offender chose privacy and it was granted immediately.

In the private conversation, separate the stated business issue from the personal one. Press the question 'so this is about you?' and let the real motivation surface (feeling underutilized, career anxiety).
Ask what contribution the person is actually making to the team, and be direct if the answer is negative, while affirming that there is a lot they have to offer.
Do not sell the person on a solution. In the source the leader resists persuading the offender into a role; a peer makes the argument instead, and the offender self-selects.
Give the offender a chance to address the team in their own words rather than apologizing on their behalf.
caveats: The source leader later admits she believed the person would quit — a public confrontation with a senior person carries real retention risk.

Correcting behavior in front of the group can itself become a morale event; the source uses the private option deliberately, except where the behavior was aimed at the leader and needed a visible response.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Confirm role fit with an assignment change before adding headcount
cards.summary: When someone is visibly underutilized and pushing projects out of personal need, test whether a change of scope — not a new acquisition or hire — resolves it.
cards.use_when: A senior team member or key contractor in the store is agitating for a big new initiative, an acquisition, a second brand or a large hire mostly because they are bored.
steps: When a big proposal arrives, ask the diagnostic questions first: what do we get — customers, employees, technology — and how many of each? In the source, the acquisition added ~20 customers, ~75 staff, and new products, roughly 50% company growth.
Separate the proposal's strategic merit from the proposer's personal need. Ask directly whether the project exists to give someone something to own.
Check whether the function whose perspective matters is in the room. Excluding marketing from a positioning decision, or fulfillment from a range decision, is itself a symptom.
Before approving big growth, confirm the company's existing operational problems wouldn't be exacerbated — in the source, politics would be made worse by absorbing a new team.

If the person is underutilized, change their assignment instead: assign ownership of the function where their existing skill is strongest and which the business actually needs (in the source, an ex-sales leader takes over sales).
Let peers make the case for the reassignment rather than the leader selling it; the person is more likely to convert when the argument comes from colleagues.
Require the reassigned person to fix the specific dysfunction they complained about — in the source, silence about priorities in their own team.
caveats: The acquisition figures in the source are fictional case detail, not a template for evaluating real deals.
A big acquisition can still be right; the source's point is the sequence — resolve internal capability and politics first, then grow.
